places.name: Chaurasi Temple Complex
places.summary: Bharmaur's 7th-century temple complex of 84 shrines around the Manimahesh Shiva temple, in the middle of town.
places.seoDescription: Chaurasi temples in Bharmaur: 84 shrines from about the 7th century, the Manimahesh Shiva temple, Lakshana Devi, the metal Nandi and the start of the Manimahesh Yatra.

images.alt: Stone shikhara temples of the Chaurasi complex in Bharmaur under green hills
images.caption: Chaurasi temples, Bharmaur

overview.text:
In the centre of Bharmaur, the Chaurasi complex gathers 84 shrines — chaurasi means eighty-four — around a courtyard. It dates to about the 7th century, from the days when Bharmaur, as Brahmapura, was the capital of Chamba State.

The main temple, to Shiva as Manimahesh, enshrines a huge linga. In front of it, in a modern shed, stands a life-size metal Nandi bull with a broken ear and tail. The oldest shrine is Lakshana Devi's, dedicated to Durga as the buffalo-slaying Mahishasuramardini; there are also temples to Narsingh, Dharmeshvar Mahadev and Ganesh near the entrance. Pilgrims on the Manimahesh Yatra start here; the lake itself is 26 km away, the last 13 km on foot from Hadsar.

places.name: Christ Church, Kasauli
places.summary: A 19th-century Anglican church in the heart of Kasauli, one of Himachal's oldest, known for its stained glass.
places.seoTitle: Christ Church, Kasauli: Colonial Church & Stained Glass
places.seoDescription: Christ Church in Kasauli: a 19th-century Anglican church from the British Raj, its stained-glass Bible scenes and its place on a walk around the Mall.

images.alt: The grey stone tower and pitched roof of Christ Church in Kasauli among trees
images.caption: Christ Church, Kasauli

overview.text:
Christ Church stands in the heart of Kasauli, a charming Anglican church built in the 19th century during the British Raj and one of the oldest churches in Himachal Pradesh. Kasauli itself began as an army cantonment in 1842, and the church is the clearest reminder of those years.

It is known for its colonial architecture and quiet atmosphere, and above all for its stained-glass windows, which show scenes from the Bible. Visit on a walk around the Mall and the old bazaars, then carry on to Monkey Point or along the Gilbert Trail, which runs through thick pine forest with views over the valleys. Lawrence School and the town's other churches are close by too.

places.name: Naggar Castle
places.summary: The old castle of the Kullu Rajas on a steep rise above the Beas, now a tourist lodge with wide valley views.
places.seoTitle: Naggar Castle: Kullu's Royal Castle Lodge
places.seoDescription: Naggar Castle above the Beas: the Kullu Rajas' old seat, built with stones from Baragarh fort, now a tourist lodge, with the Gauri Shankar temple below.

images.alt: The stone-and-timber walls and slate roof of Naggar Castle above the Kullu valley
images.caption: Naggar Castle

overview.text:
Naggar was the capital of Kullu for generations, and the massive castle of its Rajas still stands on a steep rise overlooking the valley, dominating the village and the countryside around. It is said to have been built in the reign of Raja Sidh Singh, with stones carried over from Baragarh fort on the opposite side of the valley.

The castle has since been converted into a tourist lodge, so you can stay the night or just walk in for the view across the Beas. At the foot of the small bazaar below stands the Gauri Shankar temple, a protected stone temple about 800 years old, and the Roerich estate is a short climb above.
